I grew up with DOS. I realize that most Linux distros now have lovely UIs. Even so, I feel uncomfortable not knowing how to get my hands dirty if need be. I'd like to start using Linux, but don't want to install Ubuntu/Mint/etc. and then engage with them on a strictly superficial level.

Suggestions?
Best site / book for learning Linux commands?

"The Linux Command Line": http://www.linuxcommand.org/tlcl.php (note that it's available for free download).

And the more in-depth one "Linux Command Line and Shell Scripting Bible": https://www.amazon.com/Linux-Command-Shell-Scripting-Bible/dp/111898384X

The Linux Command Line is a great book. I've been using Linux exclusively for about 2 years & disk-booting for about 3 before that; I was leaning new commands in the first 2 chapters. And they were useful commands too.

Man pages (most commands are documented right on the system) and online searches are the quickest way to find information. the post from /u/no-cheating is useful. You'll quickly find that about 99% of whatever you're trying to do has already been done, or there's one or more apps that will do it.

If you're talking about learning linux commands, I've been using unix/linux for about 28 years, and I still learn new things. The first and most important thing is to learn regular expressions and how they relate to linux commands. Learn shell scripting, and how to combine simple commands to accomplish what you are trying to do.

Books do tend to become dated. I could say the same about online searches, since a lot of the results pertain to older versions of software/operating systems.

Heres a cheatsheet for some basic commands: http://overapi.com/linux

Also check the resource box in the upper left corner for more information and distribution specific commands.

It's free and perfect to new users

http://unixmages.com/ufbm.pdf
You might want to take a look at installing Slackware and bsd unix as we'll. there is a free website called learn python the hard way that starts off with some command line tutorials as well

Hands on. Real world knowledge always beats theoretical knowledge. Take an old quadcore machine, install ProxMox, and then install a bunch of Devuan servers on it. Install a mail server, install a NFS, install a firewall, install a wiki, documenting your processes, install icinga to monitor it all, install an owncloud instance.

When you are done with all of that, you will know far more than you could have from reading a book, and it's all free, just requires time and "elbow grease".

As others have echoed, I would recommend not doing Ubuntu/Mint to start off with if this is your approach. Not because they aren't command line friendly but because they do have a lot of "easy outs" with GUIs. Go with something that requires you do more on the command line, something like Arch or Gentoo if you want to go on the hard end of the spectrum. If you want GUIs there but not quite as many but still a little more focused on command line then Fedora might be an option though it won't be much harder than Ubuntu.

Full disclosure: I'm a Fedora fan. I've tried many variants of Ubuntu, Arch a few times, even BSD at one point. They offer some great perspectives on how the same task can be dealt with. If you have the time, resources, and drive then I'd recommend trying Fedora, Arch, and FreeBSD.
